indignant

in-DIG-nunt -- stress on the second syllable, DIG. · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Indignant is angry at unfair treatment.

Fans were indignant when the league fined the injured player instead of the opponent who had tripped him.

Worked Example

A cashier is written up for money missing from a register on a night she was not even scheduled to work, and the manager refuses to look at the schedule.

Her anger is indignant: it comes from being wronged, not from ordinary irritation. Indignant anger always carries a sense of injustice behind it -- 'this is not fair, and it should not have happened to me.'

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

affronted: Affronted is the sting of a moment of open disrespect -- a rude remark, a snub delivered to your face. Indignant is anger at unfairness of any kind and on anyone's behalf. You are affronted by an insult aimed at you; you are indignant when the rules themselves are broken.

aggrieved: Aggrieved means feeling you have a genuine grievance -- a wrong you could list point by point in a formal complaint. It is quieter and more official-sounding than indignant: an aggrieved employee files a written protest, while an indignant one is already objecting out loud.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

content: calmly satisfied with how things are

unbothered: not disturbed or upset in the least

Where it sits · how loud and hot the anger burns — resentful → indignant → outraged

resentful vs. indignant: Resentful smolders where indignant flares -- a resentful person nurses the grudge quietly for months, while an indignant one objects out loud the moment the unfairness lands.

outraged vs. indignant: Outraged pushes well past indignant: an indignant customer protests being overcharged, while an outraged public demands that somebody lose their job over it.

Build the Word

The pieces

prefix — in-

prefix — in-: not (Latin in-)

root — dign-

root — dign-: worthy (Latin dignus 'worthy')

suffix — -ant

suffix — -ant: forms an adjective: being in that state (Latin -antem, via Old French)

Put it together

Put it together: Indignant carries this unit's prefix in- ('not') in front of Latin dignus ('worthy'): to be indignant is to burn at being treated as though you were not worthy of fair treatment. Note the honest limit here -- 'dign' is not a standalone English word, so the split is likely rather than airtight, but the root is unmistakable once you see dignity, dignify, and deign standing beside it.

Use the root in a new word: dignity

Use the root in a new word: dignity: She answered the insult with quiet dignity and kept walking.

Root Check

Word Choice

Indignant is not plain anger -- it is anger with a cause. Save it for injustice: an indignant letter, an indignant protest, indignant parents. Its noun is indignation, and 'righteous indignation' is the standard phrase. Watch out for the look-alike indigent, which means 'very poor' and has nothing to do with anger at all.
